transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes (recording ended at 15:58)
Location: Zoom
Recording id: ff-2026-04-06-bba-warmstart-001

Attendees:
- Avery Chen (Redwood AE)
- Marcus Li (Redwood SE)
- Emma Torres (BlueBay)
- Liam O'Connor (BlueBay SRE)
- Nina Park (BlueBay CTO)

Summary:
Short technical deep dive to validate observed warmstart vs steady-state perf differences between TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) and vLLM on BlueBay's on-prem VPC cluster. Focus areas: kernel selection differences under varying sequence lengths, CUDA-graph capture/replay stability, KV cache priming effects (they say KV cash in one note), and quantized INT8 behavior under mixed-batch workloads. Goal was to agree on an experiment matrix for a pilot.

Topics covered:
- Warm start (cold cache -> steady state) latency skew
- CUDA graph replay nondeterminism when capture sequence length diverges
- Kernel path switches and eviction behavior when KV cache is primed vs miss-heavy
- TensorRT-LLM deterministic kernels vs vLLM dynamic scheduler tradeoffs
- INT8 quantization artifacts vs FP16 in throughput-sensitive scenarios
- VPC/on-prem constraints (KMS, storage mounts, SSO) that affect cold-resources and primes

Transcript (timestamps are approximate):
[00:00] Avery: ok, thanks for joining everyone, uh quick intros then we'll dive in. Avery from Redwood, Marcus our performance SE.
[00:12] Emma: hey thanks, excited, weve been seeing a weird delta between our nightly bench and steady run, so wanted to understand where the warmstart hit is coming from.
[00:18] Marcus: yeah, and to be clear, we ran both TRT-LLM and vLLM on the same machine image right? same model checkpoint?
[00:22] Emma: correct same fp16 checkpoint, except we also tried an INT8 quant build for TRT-LLM.
[00:28] Marcus: ok good, that helps. quick overview: TRT-LLM tends to choose fused kernels and relies heavily on cuda-graph capture for the steady-state path, whereas vLLM does more dynamic kernel scheduling and smaller kernels that can adapt to sequence length. that can cause warmstart vs steady divergence.
[00:45] Liam: can you expand on the cuda-graph fragility? we saw occasional stalls when sequence length changes mid-batch during capture replay.
[00:51] Marcus: yes, we saw that too. nvprof traces show that when capture length Lcap != actual Lrun the replay may trigger fallback to the slower graphless path, or in some cases theres a short misalignment where kernels are recompiled, causing a 40-200ms spike. in TRT-LLM the graph replay is usually faster but brittle.
[01:12] Nina: is that the same with INT8? our INT8 runs had sporadic quality diffs, also more spikes.
[01:18] Marcus: INT8 adds another axis—calibration and kernel selection can change; some fused INT8 kernels are chosen only for certain shapes. so when batches interleave shapes (prompt lengths) you can flip kernel selection and blow the nvtx timeline.
[01:30] Emma: we called them "shape flips" in our notes, yep. question: what about KV cache priming? we saw initial requests 5-10x slower until the cache warms.
[01:38] Avery: KV cache priming is critical. if the first request misses the prefix cache you pay a full KV-read + memcopy and potentially a different kernel path. can you describe your traffic pattern?
[01:46] Emma: mostly chatty at low QPS, many short sessions, P50 latency target is 120ms but P95 we want under 400ms; bursts up to 60 QPS.
[01:56] Marcus: low QPS + many new sessions = more cold starts and KV misses. recommended: prefix caching (long TTL) and background priming of common prefixes, or a tiny warm pool of pinned containers that maintain KV. that reduces the warm delta.
[02:10] Liam: for on-prem VPC, we noticed mount latency to our shared KV store (NFS-ish) adds 30-60ms occasionally. does Redwood support local pinned KV or in-GPU persistent cache?
[02:18] Avery: yes we support in-GPU persistent KV and optional local SSD-backed cache on the node. for private deployments we can configure a hot KV shard on the same machine to avoid NFS hops.
[02:28] Marcus: note there are memory pressure effects. if the node runs multiple tenants the persistent KV can get evicted, causing those same warm spikes. during the call we saw eviction thrashing in the long-run trace.
[02:40] Emma: do you have a recommendation for memory allocation? we have ~80GB GPU and currently run 2 workers per card.
[02:46] Marcus: for your workload I'd suggest a single worker pop with multiple lanes; that keeps the KV resident and reduces cross-process copies. also reserve a percentage for the persistent KV (say 10-15% of device RAM).
[02:58] Nina: ok that might complicate our multi-tenant usage, we'll need to think about dedicated pools.
[03:03] Marcus: yep, Dedicated reservation or Dedicated pools help.
[03:06] Emma: back to TRT vs vLLM: we saw TRT have lower steady throughput but worse spikes on shape flips; vLLM had slightly higher P95 but more consistent. which should we pick?
[03:16] Marcus: it's tradeoffs—TRT wins when you can standardize shape and use graph capture, vLLM is more robust to variable seq lengths. since you have many short sessions and variable lengths, vLLM may be simpler for initial pilot; TRT-LLM could be used for high-throughput stable routes.
[03:30] Avery: add quantization into that decision: INT8 on TRT can give large throughput gains but increases kernel fragility and the risk of calibration regressions. while FP16 on TRT is more stable.
[03:42] Emma: we also logged correctness diffs on INT8 at tail tokens, any suggestions?
[03:47] Marcus: collect a small eval set and run the INT8 calibration + post-calibration eval. if you see quality drift correlate with certain tokens/positions then INT8 might be risky for customer-facing production.
[03:58] Liam: can we instrument kernel handoff events in the runtime? we want to correlate those to spikes automatically.
[04:03] Marcus: yes, Redwood runtime emits a kernel-path telemetry event and NVTX markers; we'll add tracepoint mapping that maps timestamps to kernel selection. Marcus: that's one of the action items.
[04:12] Emma: about cuda-graph capture: are you suggesting capture per-batch-shape or a generic larger capture?
[04:18] Marcus: capture per principal shape is safest. a wildcard capture that tries to cover many shapes tends to produce lots of fallback scenarios. heuristics: capture for the top 2-3 most frequent lengths and let vLLM handle the rest.
[04:33] Nina: for the VPC private deployment we need security notes: KMS integrations, SOC2 audit, RBAC in the console. will Redwood provide docs?
[04:41] Avery: yes we'll send the security pack and the private deployment checklist; we already discussed KMS/HSM options in the initial docs. Avery: I'll attach it to the follow-up.
[04:51] Emma: great. another oddity: when we used cudagraph replay with mixed precision it seemed to sometimes misalign on multi-gpu NVLINK machines; traces showed different kernel order on GPU1 vs GPU0.
[05:00] Marcus: multi-GPU NVLINK replication can expose ordering issues, especially when graphs are captured per-device independently. recommended: synchronized capture across devices or prefer the dynamic path for interleaved multi-gpu workloads until we validate replay determinism.
[05:15] Emma: ok. any quick wins we can apply before the pilot?
[05:18] Marcus: yes: 1) increase KV TTL for common prefixes, 2) pin a tiny warm pool (1-2 containers) to keep persistent KV warm, 3) pre-capture graphs for your top 2 lengths in TRT-LLM, 4) if using INT8, run a conservative eval and hold back quant for sensitive routes.
[05:34] Avery: to add, we'll give you a configuration diff for your on-prem node to set the GPU reserved memory and lane counts.
[05:41] Emma: thanks, that sounds good. also can you explain the memory tradeoffs for single worker vs multi worker again?
[05:46] Marcus: single worker with many lanes means one process keeps KV resident in GPU memory; multi-worker isolates faults but duplicates KV memory per process. so single worker reduces memory footprint and avoids cross-process copies at the cost of process-level isolation.
[06:02] Liam: are there recommended kernel reproducers we can run? small harness?
[06:07] Marcus: yes, we'll push a small harness (python + nvtx + cudagraph toggle) that runs over your prompt set. it's lightweight and will produce a csv of kernel selections and timing.
[06:18] Nina: timeline for pilot? our Q2 budget review is April 20, we want a proposal before then.
[06:24] Avery: ok we'll aim to have the summary, experiment matrix and SOW draft in about one week.
[06:29] Emma: cool. small nit: transcription shows "KV cash" in our notes, haha.
[06:34] Marcus: classic.

[06:36] Recap and next steps:
- Marcus: run microbench suite (warm/cold runs, nvprof, cuda-graph on/off) and upload traces.
- Emma: share prompt set and latency targets.
- Avery: send security pack and pilot SOW + recommended node config.

[06:50] Closing: thanks everyone; we'll sync next week to review traces.
